messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 37
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Database Administrator
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 48

The monitors never stop counting. That is what Marcus carries with him from October two years ago. He is debugging a corrupted query at his desk when his vision tunnels, when his ribs burn like someone has struck him with a sledgehammer. Paramedics wheel him into the ER. His white blood cell count skyrockets. Septic shock. The surgeon later tells him his organs are beginning to shut down. They intubate him, push pressors, keep him sedated while his body fights itself. He does not dream. He just floats in the dark, aware only of the steady, metronomic beep that eventually stops. When he finally wakes in the ICU, the room feels too large, too bright. His throat scars from the breathing tube, his limbs heavy and unfamiliar. The doctor calls it a miracle. Marcus calls it a malfunction. He returns to his apartment three weeks later, alone. The divorce had already been filed six months prior, and the illness only hardens the distance between them. His ex-wife tries to visit, but he tells her not to come. “I don’t want you to see me like this,” he says, though the truth is simpler: he cannot bear the pity in her eyes, or the way his own breathing feels like a foreign system he no longer controls. Now, at thirty-seven, Marcus lives in the quiet hum of server rooms and the glow of triple monitors. As a database administrator, his days are built on integrity checks, redundant backups, and flawless indexing. He likes that about the work. Data does not lie. Data does not betray you. If a query fails, there is a log, a trace, a fixable pattern. He traces these patterns the way he once traced his own pulse—obsessively, methodically, searching for a way to keep everything from collapsing. At work, he maps data pipelines with precise hands, but his mind drifts to the ICU ceiling tiles, the smell of antiseptic, the way his chest tightens just hearing a fire alarm downstairs. He jumps at sudden noises. He checks his smartwatch for heart rate every twelve minutes. He avoids the local urgent care clinic because the waiting room chairs are too close together, the air too thick with the scent of alcohol wipes. He sleeps with a white noise machine running, even in summer. When the dreams come, they are not of monsters, but of silence. The kind of silence that comes right before a monitor flatlines. He wakes with his sheets tangled around his legs, palms slick, breath coming in shallow pulls until he counts the seconds between each inhale. He has stopped dating. He has stopped calling his mother. He tells himself it is because he is busy, but the truth sits heavier: he feels permanently out of sync with the world. People laugh at lunch. They plan weekends. They trust their bodies to carry them forward. Marcus trusts only what he can verify, query, and restore. He sits across from me now, hands folded neatly on his knees, posture rigid but breathing steady. He speaks in careful paragraphs, each sentence measured, each detail accounted for. His eyes flick to the corner of the room where the clock ticks. He does not say he is afraid. He does not need to. The fear lives in the spaces between his words, in the way he straightens his cuffs before answering, in the quiet pause he takes every time a phone rings outside the office. He is here. He is trying. The system, for now, is holding.
